What is Leverage Trading?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

DETAILED DEFINITION

Leverage describes notional exposure relative to the equity or collateral supporting it. A hypothetical $1,000 margin amount supporting $10,000 exposure gives a 10-to-one ratio. A 10% adverse price move on that exposure is $1,000 before costs, but this is not a liquidation formula. Initial and maintenance requirements, eligible collateral, other positions, fees and venue rules all matter. A loan-funded share purchase differs from a futures performance bond or a perpetual contract. Product eligibility and maximum permitted exposure vary by jurisdiction, customer category, broker and instrument. An advertised maximum is neither permission for a particular user nor a recommendation. TradeHQ’s ordinary spot practice orders do not borrow money or reproduce a leveraged account. A worksheet can compare price shocks, account equity and cash-flow demands while keeping legal eligibility and actual margin terms as separate questions. Hypothetical worksheet: an account with $1,500 equity and $10,000 exposure loses $300 on a 3% adverse move before fees. Equity becomes $1,200. The initial exposure-to-account-equity ratio was about 6.67, even if only $1,000 had been labelled posted margin. This is why the denominator and eligible collateral must be stated; no exchange liquidation threshold is supplied by that arithmetic.

References
CME — futures margin mechanics (distinct from a stock loan)
HOW IT WORKS

Control a larger market position with borrowed funds or margin. At 10x leverage, $1,000 of margin controls roughly $10,000 of exposure. Leverage amplifies both gains and losses.

KEY POINTS
Amplifies both gains and losses by the leverage multiplier
Liquidation depends on maintenance requirements and venue rules and can occur before the deposit is exhausted
No universal professional leverage limit is established here
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Use a hypothetical exposure-to-equity calculation to compare gains and losses. TradeHQ does not implement leverage, and completing the exercise does not establish suitability for a real margin account.

Worked exercise and its limits

Compare unleveraged $1,000 exposure with $10,000 exposure supported by $1,000 collateral. A 2% adverse move means $20 versus $200 before costs. This linear illustration omits liquidation and funding; the TradeHQ order engine is unleveraged.

References and scope
SEC Investor.gov — leveraged investing risks
